opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a lot of real progress underneath the hype, but the hype is still running ahead of where the technology actually is. Having spent years building robots before coming to work on language models, my honest take is that people tend to underestimate how hard the last stretch of reliability is in the physical world.

What's genuinely exciting is that foundation models have changed the shape of the problem. Before, you had to hand-engineer perception, planning, and control for every single task, and that made generalization almost impossible. Now you can get a robot to understand a fairly open-ended instruction, recognize objects it's never seen, and reason about what to do. That's a real step change, and the demos you see are mostly not fake. Those things really can happen.

The catch is that a demo that works 80% of the time and a product that works 99.9% of the time are separated by an enormous amount of work. In software, if an agent fails, you retry, or a human looks at the diff. In robotics, failure means a dropped dish, a damaged part, or someone getting hurt. And you can't just spin up a million copies in the cloud to collect data. Every data point costs real hardware time, real resets, real wear and tear. So the data flywheel that made language models so powerful is much slower and more expensive to get going for physical systems.

So I'd say: be bullish on the long term, and a bit skeptical of timelines. I think we'll see real deployments first in fairly structured settings like warehouses, logistics, and specific manufacturing tasks, where the environment is constrained and the economic value is clear. The general-purpose humanoid that walks into your home and does your laundry reliably is coming, but I think it's further away than a lot of the funding announcements would suggest. The interesting question to me is less "will it happen" and more "what's the path to collecting enough real-world data to close that reliability gap."

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's a mix of justified excitement and a lot of overshooting on timelines. I spent years at Cobalt Robotics building and deploying security robots into real buildings, and the thing that experience burns into you is that the demo is maybe five percent of the work. Anyone can get a robot to do something impressive once, in a controlled space, with the right lighting and a team of engineers standing just off camera. Getting it to do that thing ten thousand times, in a building you've never seen, when the elevator is broken and someone left a mop bucket in the hallway, is a completely different problem.

What's genuinely new, and why I don't dismiss the hype, is that the perception and reasoning side has gotten dramatically better. When I was working on robots, the hardest part was often just the robot understanding what it was looking at and what it should do when something unexpected happened. Large models are a real step change there. A robot can now look at a scene and have some commonsense notion of what's going on, and that was basically science fiction a few years ago.

But the hardware and the reliability problem haven't gotten easier at the same rate. Hands are still really hard. Batteries are still heavy. Things break. And the economics are brutal, because a robot doing a task has to compete with a human who costs a certain amount per hour and comes with built-in reliability and an incredible general-purpose body. The humanoid videos are exciting, but I'd want to see cost per useful hour of work before I believed the timelines people are throwing around.

So my assessment is that the direction is right and the enthusiasm is directionally correct, but the people saying general-purpose humanoids in your home in two or three years are underestimating the long tail. I'd expect narrow, boring deployments to succeed first, the same way it worked with earlier waves of robotics, and the broad stuff to take longer than the demos suggest.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robotics demos, deployment challenges, and timelines, but does not compare AI robotics to self-driving cars roughly ten years earlier.

r002.rationale: It says a demo is only a small part of the work, describes the difficulty of reliable operation across real-world settings, and expects broad deployments to take longer than demos suggest.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of real progress, but people often underestimate the gap between a compelling demo and a useful product. With robotics, you need to ask: How often does it work? What happens when it fails? And how much human intervention is happening behind the scenes?

The exciting part is that AI could make robots much more adaptable. Instead of programming every individual motion for a very specific environment, you can start giving them higher-level instructions. But that doesn’t eliminate the hardware challenges or the need for reliability.

So I’m optimistic about the direction. I’m more skeptical of timelines that jump straight from a robot doing something impressive in a video to a robot doing useful work all day without supervision. That’s where a lot of the hard engineering lives.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the gap between demos and useful products but does not compare AI robotics with self-driving cars ten years earlier.

r002.rationale: It expresses skepticism about timelines that jump directly from demos to unsupervised work, but does not clearly state that widespread deployment can take a long time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s real progress underneath the hype, but people often underestimate the gap between an impressive demo and a robot that’s useful every day. A demo shows that something can work. A product has to work reliably across all the messy situations you didn’t anticipate, and at a cost that makes sense.

What’s exciting is the possibility that we can reuse more of the intelligence across tasks, instead of engineering each behavior separately. But you still have the physical constraints: hardware breaks, collecting data takes time, and mistakes can be expensive. So I’m optimistic about the direction, but I’d judge the progress by how much useful work robots do with how little human intervention, rather than by how compelling the videos are.
